title: Strategy Pattern
tagline: Swap algorithms at runtime without changing the code that uses them — compose behaviour, don't inherit it.

sections.content:
**Problem:** You have a `Checkout` class that needs to support Stripe, PayPal, and crypto payments. The naive solution: a giant `if/else` or `switch` block inside `Checkout.pay()`. Every time a new payment method is added, you reopen and edit `Checkout` — violating the Open/Closed Principle and tangling unrelated algorithms in one class.

**Core idea:** The **Strategy** pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one in its own class, and makes them interchangeable. The **Context** (e.g., `Checkout`) holds a reference to a **Strategy** object and delegates work to it. The context doesn't know — or care — which concrete strategy is active. Strategies are swappable at runtime, testable in isolation, and addable without touching existing code.

sections.caption: Context delegates to whichever Strategy is currently set. New strategies are added without touching Context.

sections.title: A GPS App with Multiple Routes
sections.content:
A navigation app has one destination but multiple route strategies: fastest, shortest, scenic, avoid tolls. The map screen (Context) doesn't hard-code directions — it delegates to whatever **routing strategy** is selected. Switching from 'fastest' to 'avoid tolls' doesn't rewrite the map screen; it just swaps the strategy object.

This is exactly how JavaScript's `Array.sort(compareFn)` works: the sorting algorithm is fixed, but the **comparison strategy** is injected — `sort((a,b) => a.age - b.age)` vs `sort((a,b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))`. The array doesn't change; the strategy does.

**Participants:**

- **Strategy** — an interface (or duck-typed contract) with a single method, e.g., `execute(data)`. All concrete strategies implement this method.
- **ConcreteStrategy** — a self-contained algorithm. `StripeStrategy.execute()` calls the Stripe SDK; `CryptoStrategy.execute()` broadcasts a blockchain transaction. Each is independently testable.
- **Context** — owns a reference to the current strategy via `setStrategy(s)`. Its public API (`checkout.pay(amount)`) delegates to `this._strategy.execute(amount)`. The context is never aware of how the algorithm works.

**Compile-time vs Runtime selection:** Strategies can be selected at startup from config (`process.env.PAYMENT_PROVIDER`) or switched mid-session (user changes payment method in the UI). Both are transparent to the Context.

**Strategy vs Inheritance:** Without the pattern you might subclass `Checkout` into `StripeCheckout`, `PayPalCheckout`, etc. Subclassing is static — you cannot switch algorithms at runtime. Strategy uses **composition** (`_strategy` field) instead of inheritance, making it far more flexible.

**Strategy vs Command:** Both encapsulate behaviour in an object. Strategy replaces a whole algorithm (one variant at a time); Command encapsulates a request that can be queued, logged, or undone (multiple commands can be stacked).

**In the wild:** `Array.sort(compareFn)`, Passport.js authentication strategies, webpack loaders, Lodash's `_.sortBy`, form validators (Yup schemas as interchangeable validation strategies).

sections.caption: The Context routes to one strategy at a time. Adding a new payment method = adding one new branch and class, zero changes to Context.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Payment strategies are plain objects with a `pay()` method — no class hierarchy needed in JavaScript. `setStrategy()` swaps the algorithm at runtime. The `Array.sort(compareFn)` block shows the pattern built into the language.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: Clean skeleton showing strategy selection logic separated from the Context. The context is oblivious to which algorithm runs — it only calls execute().

sections.content:
**When to use:** Multiple variants of an algorithm that need to be selected at runtime; when `if/switch` branching on type is growing; when you want to test algorithms in isolation.

**When NOT to use:** If you only have one algorithm, the abstraction adds noise. If strategies share no interface at all, a factory function may be simpler.

**Trade-off:** Clients must be aware that strategies exist and must configure the context — this adds a layer of knowledge. Mitigate with a factory or dependency injection container.

**Real frameworks:** Passport.js (`passport.use(new LocalStrategy(...))`), webpack loaders/plugins, Joi/Yup validators, `Array.sort(compareFn)`, `Intl.Collator` as a locale comparison strategy.

items: **Compose over inherit:** Strategy uses a `_strategy` field (composition) rather than subclassing, enabling runtime algorithm swapping.
**Open/Closed:** Adding a new algorithm = adding a new strategy class/object; the Context never changes.
**Testability:** Each strategy is a self-contained unit — mock the context, inject the strategy under test.
**JS idiom:** In JavaScript, any function or object with the right method signature qualifies — no need for formal abstract classes.
**Array.sort(compareFn) is Strategy:** The built-in sort is the most ubiquitous example of the pattern in everyday JavaScript.

quiz.question: What is the primary problem the Strategy pattern solves?
options: Preventing multiple objects from receiving the same event.
Eliminating a growing if/switch block of algorithm variants inside the Context.
Ensuring only one instance of a class exists.
Providing a simplified interface to a complex subsystem.
quiz.explanation: Strategy extracts each algorithm variant into its own object, eliminating branching logic inside the context and making adding new variants non-invasive.

quiz.question: Which JavaScript built-in API is the most direct everyday example of the Strategy pattern?
options: JSON.stringify(value, replacer)
Array.prototype.sort(compareFn)
Promise.race(promises)
Object.keys(obj)
quiz.explanation: Array.sort(compareFn) takes a comparison strategy as a parameter. The sorting algorithm is fixed; the comparison logic is the injected strategy.

quiz.question: How does Strategy differ from subclassing to vary behaviour?
options: Strategy is slower because it uses delegation.
Subclassing allows runtime swapping; Strategy does not.
Strategy uses composition (a _strategy field) enabling runtime swapping; subclassing is static.
Strategy requires a formal abstract base class; subclassing does not.
quiz.explanation: Composition via a field allows the algorithm to be swapped at runtime (setStrategy()). Inheritance is a compile-time decision — you cannot change a subclass at runtime.

quiz.question: In Passport.js, what plays the role of 'Strategy'?
options: The Express app object.
The req.user property.
The authentication algorithm objects passed to passport.use() (e.g., LocalStrategy, JwtStrategy).
The session middleware.
quiz.explanation: Passport.use(new LocalStrategy(...)) registers a concrete strategy. Passport is the Context — it delegates authentication to whichever strategy is active.

quiz.question: What does Context.setStrategy(s) allow that subclassing does not?
options: Access to private fields of the strategy.
Swapping the algorithm at runtime without creating a new Context object.
Calling multiple strategies simultaneously.
Inheriting state from the previous strategy.
quiz.explanation: setStrategy() replaces the _strategy reference mid-lifecycle — the same Context object uses a different algorithm from that point onward.

quiz.question: Which principle does the Strategy pattern most directly satisfy?
options: Liskov Substitution Principle
Single Responsibility Principle
Open/Closed Principle
Interface Segregation Principle
quiz.explanation: Adding a new algorithm requires only adding a new Strategy class — the Context is never modified. Open for extension, closed for modification.

quiz.question: What is the key structural difference between Strategy and Command?
options: Strategy objects can be undone; Command objects cannot.
Strategy replaces a whole algorithm (one active at a time); Command encapsulates a request that can be queued, logged, or undone.
Command uses composition; Strategy uses inheritance.
They are identical patterns with different names.
quiz.explanation: Strategy = interchangeable algorithm (mutually exclusive). Command = encapsulated request that can stack, queue, and reverse. Different intents.

quiz.question: In JavaScript, what is the minimum requirement for an object to qualify as a Strategy?
options: It must extend a base Strategy class.
It must be decorated with a @Strategy annotation.
It must implement the method signature the Context expects (duck typing).
It must be a singleton.
quiz.explanation: JavaScript is duck-typed. Any object or function that satisfies the expected interface (e.g., has a pay() method) qualifies as a strategy — no formal inheritance required.

quiz.question: When is the Strategy pattern NOT a good fit?
options: When the number of algorithm variants may grow over time.
When algorithms must be selected based on runtime configuration.
When there is only a single algorithm and no variants are anticipated.
When algorithms need to be unit-tested in isolation.
quiz.explanation: YAGNI — if there is only one algorithm, extracting it into a strategy object adds indirection with no benefit. Introduce the pattern when a second variant appears.

quiz.question: A Checkout class receives a payment strategy through its constructor. What dependency injection benefit does this provide?
options: The Checkout class can now extend multiple strategy classes.
Tests can inject a fake strategy without hitting real payment APIs.
The strategy is automatically selected based on environment variables.
The Checkout class becomes a singleton.
quiz.explanation: Injecting the strategy as a constructor argument allows tests to pass a simple mock object (e.g., { pay: () => ({ success: true }) }) — no real Stripe or PayPal calls.
